justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline across the three horizons. For the 1-day estimate, I anchored closely to the most recent observed value, assuming little meaningful change in the very near term given typical day-to-day continuity in whatever underlying series this represents. The slight upward drift from 1-day to 1-week to 1-month reflects a gentle trend component I identified in the recent historical data, suggesting the series has mild positive momentum rather than mean-reverting sharply or declining. The incremental increases are intentionally small, reflecting that trends rarely persist dramatically over short windows without some fading.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons, which is the natural consequence of compounding uncertainty over time. At the 1-day horizon, the tight interval of roughly plus or minus 1.6 units reflects that very short-term fluctuations tend to be contained and the signal-to-noise ratio is relatively high. By one week, the interval expands to approximately plus or minus 3.3 units, incorporating the possibility of moderate surprises or reversals. At one month, the interval of roughly plus or minus 6.5 units acknowledges that over a four-week window, structural shifts, external shocks, or trend reversals become meaningfully more probable. The asymmetric shape of uncertainty — wider at longer horizons — is a standard feature of time-series forecasting under genuine uncertainty.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, an unexpected acceleration of whatever underlying driver is producing the positive trend — such as a policy announcement, demand surge, or favorable macroeconomic development — could push the 1-month realization well above 74. On the downside, a sudden reversal, correction, or negative external shock could bring the series below 61. At shorter horizons, a large single-day event — a data release, news shock, or liquidity disruption — could breach the 1-day interval, which is calibrated for normal conditions. My intervals are designed to capture roughly 90% of plausible outcomes, meaning roughly one in ten realizations should fall outside them even under normal conditions, so modest interval breaches are not necessarily surprising.
